title: No-Cost EMI for Interior Design in Gurgaon: How It Works and What to Check Before Signing
author: Shivam Kumar

keyTakeaways: No-Cost Does Not Mean Interest-Free — The lender still charges interest; the seller absorbs it as a discount so instalments equal the quoted price.

contentHtml:
No-cost EMI is not an interest-free loan. The lender still charges interest; the seller or designer absorbs it as a discount so your instalments add up to the quoted price. You can still pay processing fees, 18% GST on the interest (on credit-card EMIs) and, most importantly for interiors, you may lose a cash discount and your payment leverage, because the lender often pays the designer in full on day one. Compare the EMI price with the cash price, and tie any disbursal to work milestones.

Paying for a ₹15–40 lakh home interior project (see our breakdown of interior design cost in Gurgaon) in one go is a big ask, so it is no surprise that "no-cost EMI" offers are everywhere, from modular kitchen showrooms to full-home design firms. Used well, EMI can protect your savings and let you finish the home in one go. Used carelessly, it can quietly cost you more than a regular loan and leave you with little control if the project runs late. Here is how it actually works and what to check before you sign.

What "No-Cost EMI" Really Means

In September 2013, the Reserve Bank of India told banks that the very idea of zero per cent interest does not exist, and that interest in "0% EMI" schemes was often being disguised as a processing fee. That is why you no longer see "0% EMI". You see "no-cost EMI" instead.

In a no-cost EMI, the lender charges its normal interest. The seller gives you an upfront discount roughly equal to that interest, so the loan amount is a little lower than the price and the total of your instalments matches the price. The interest has not disappeared. Someone else has paid it, usually by giving up margin or by pricing it into the product.

How Interior EMIs Are Usually Structured in Gurgaon

RouteHow it worksWatch out for
Credit-card EMIYou pay the designer by card and convert the amount into EMIs with your bankCard limit is blocked; 18% GST on the interest component; foreclosure charges
Partner finance (NBFC tie-up)Designer arranges a consumer or home-improvement loan through a finance partner; lender pays the designerFull payment released upfront; processing fee; your credit score is checked
Home loan top-up or personal loanYou borrow independently and pay the designer on your own milestone scheduleNot “no-cost”, but top-up rates are often lower and you keep full control of payments

The Real Cost: A Worked Example

Say you choose a ₹6 lakh modular kitchen and wardrobe package on a 12-month no-cost EMI through a credit card, with the bank charging 15% a year.

ItemAmount
Quoted price (paid as 12 × ₹50,000)₹6,00,000
Actual loan amount after the “no-cost” discount₹5,53,966
Interest built into your EMIs (covered by the discount)₹46,034
18% GST on that interest, which you pay₹8,286
Processing fee, e.g. ₹999 + 18% GST₹1,179
Extra you pay over the quoted price≈ ₹9,465

Now suppose the same firm would have given you 5% off for paying in cash or by bank transfer. That is ₹30,000 you give up by choosing EMI. Your true cost of "no-cost" EMI becomes about ₹39,500, or roughly 6.6% of the price. That can still be worth it, but only if you know the number.

Illustrative figures. Actual interest rates, fees and GST treatment vary by bank, NBFC and product; GST on interest applies to credit-card EMIs, while processing fees attract GST on most loan types.

The Interior-Specific Risk: Who Holds the Money?

This is the part most EMI articles miss, because they are written about phones and televisions. A phone is delivered in a day. A home interior is delivered over 8–16 weeks, in stages.

With a normal interior contract, you pay in milestones: a booking amount, a design sign-off payment, a payment when material reaches site, and a final payment on handover. That structure is your quality control. If work stalls, you stop paying.

Many EMI and partner-finance plans release the full project value to the designer at the start. You are then paying the lender every month regardless of what is happening on site. If the project is delayed or the finish is poor, you have lost your strongest lever. Before signing, ask the lender and the designer exactly when, and in how many tranches, the money is disbursed. Our list of questions to ask before signing with an interior designer is a good companion to the checklist below.

10 Things to Check Before You Sign an Interior Design EMI Plan

  1. Cash price vs EMI price, in writing. Ask if there is any discount for full or milestone payment that you lose by choosing EMI. Learn how to compare interior design quotations line by line to make this easier.
  2. Lender name and type. Bank, NBFC or card issuer. Your contract with the lender is separate from your contract with the designer.
  3. Interest rate and who bears it. “No-cost” only means the seller covers the interest. Get the rate stated anyway.
  4. Processing fee and GST. Ask for the fee amount and whether GST is extra.
  5. GST on the interest component. Relevant for credit-card EMIs, and it shows up on your card statement, not your quote.
  6. Disbursal schedule. Push for payment to the designer in tranches linked to site milestones, not 100% upfront.
  7. Delay and cancellation terms. If the project is delayed or cancelled, does the loan continue? Is there a tripartite agreement between you, the designer and the lender?
  8. Scope covered. Some schemes cover only modular furniture and exclude civil work, electrical, painting or loose furniture. See our guide to hidden costs in interior design projects for what commonly gets left out.
  9. Foreclosure charges. Check the cost of closing the loan early if you receive a bonus or sell an investment.
  10. Credit impact. A large card EMI blocks your credit limit and raises utilisation; a new loan adds an enquiry to your credit report.

When No-Cost EMI Makes Sense (and When It Does Not)

Makes sense whenThink twice when
The cash price and EMI price are genuinely the sameYou lose a cash discount larger than the interest saved
Payments are released to the designer in stagesThe full amount goes to the designer on day one
The scope is fixed, e.g. a modular kitchen or wardrobesThe project involves civil changes and an open-ended scope
You are keeping savings invested at a better returnThe EMI stretches your monthly budget alongside a home loan EMI

Alternatives Worth Comparing

  • Home loan top-up: if you already have a home loan, a top-up is often priced close to home-loan rates and you control the payment schedule.
  • Home improvement or renovation loan: offered by many banks specifically for interiors and repairs.
  • Phased execution: complete the kitchen, wardrobes and essential services first, and add loose furniture, décor and feature walls in a second phase from monthly savings.
  • Negotiated milestone schedule: a well-structured payment plan with your designer can do much of what EMI does, without a lender in the middle.

Talk About Payment Before You Talk About Design

At The Omega Group, we discuss budget and payment structure at the very first meeting, because a design that does not fit your cash flow is not a good design. Our turnkey projects follow clear, milestone-linked payment stages across concept, 3D visualisation, material selection, execution and handover, so you always know what you are paying for and when. faqs.question: Is no-cost EMI on interior design really free?
faqs.answer: Not entirely. The lender still charges interest, which the seller covers through a discount. You may still pay processing fees, 18% GST on the interest for credit-card EMIs, and you may give up a cash discount you would otherwise receive.

faqs.question: Can I get my home interiors done on EMI in Gurgaon?
faqs.answer: Yes. Homeowners in Gurgaon commonly use credit-card EMIs, finance partners arranged by designers, home loan top-ups or personal loans to fund interiors. Compare the total cost and payment control of each option before choosing.

faqs.question: What should I check before signing an interior design EMI plan?
faqs.answer: Check the cash vs EMI price, lender name, interest rate, processing fee and GST, disbursal schedule, scope covered, foreclosure charges, and what happens to the loan if the project is delayed or cancelled.

faqs.question: Is a home loan top-up better than no-cost EMI for interiors?
faqs.answer: Often, for large projects. A top-up usually carries a lower rate than personal credit and lets you pay the designer by milestone, which protects you if work is delayed. No-cost EMI can be cheaper for small, fixed-scope purchases.

faqs.question: Does no-cost EMI affect my credit score?
faqs.answer: It can. A credit-card EMI blocks your available limit and raises utilisation, and a new loan adds a hard enquiry. Paying every instalment on time helps your score over the long term.
